description: Moral orientation tags for concrete regulatory requirements, used as a descriptive analytical lens over AI instruments. Each requirement carries independent 0-3 salience on actor, action, and outcome. Pure forms are rare; most instruments mix all three. This file is hand-authored. Instrument-level rollups and ontology edges are derived by build/generate_knowledge_layer.py.  A requirement with moral_profile null is an obligation record that has not been tagged on actor, action, and outcome.
caveats: Pure actor, action, or outcome regimes are rare; most national and international rules are hybrids.
A single provision can carry material weight on more than one dimension; salience scores are independent, not a partition that sums to 1.
International soft law (notably OECD AI Principles 1.4) sits above or alongside national rules and is itself pluralist.
These tags describe regulatory orientation. They do not claim that any country or agency is morally one type.
Salience is an author judgment grounded in the cited text, not a measured quantity. Treat scores as ordinal, not interval.

actor.name: Actor
actor.focus: Character, duties, and competence of the people or organizations who develop, deploy, or oversee AI.
typical_signals: due diligence on developers or providers

action.name: Action
action.focus: Rightness of the act itself, independent of realized harm (deontological).

outcome.name: Outcome
outcome.focus: Foreseeable or actual impacts and harms (consequentialist).

salience_scale.1: Incidental: present but not the organizing logic
salience_scale.2: Material: a real obligation under this requirement
salience_scale.3: Defining: the primary moral orientation of this requirement

rollup_rule: For each instrument, each dimension's rollup salience is the maximum salience among that instrument's tagged requirements. Max preserves the signal that an instrument contains a strongly action-oriented (or outcome-oriented) duty somewhere, without averaging it away.

requirements.title: AI literacy
requirements.summary: Providers and deployers must take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff and of other people who operate or use AI systems on their behalf. The measures take account of those people's technical knowledge, experience, education and training, the context in which the systems are used, and the people or groups on whom the systems are used. The duty does not require a guaranteed literacy level for any individual. The Commission and the Member States support that work, including with practical examples for SMEs. The Board adopts recommendations that set common objectives.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaced Article 4. The consolidated text marks that replacement immediately before the article.

requirements.title: Prohibited AI practices
requirements.summary: Absolute bans on specified AI practices (for example social scoring by public authorities, certain biometric categorization, untargeted scraping for facial recognition databases).

moral_profile.rationale: The duty is not to perform the listed acts. Claimed benefits do not reopen the ban. Actor duties (who must refrain) and outcome concerns (why these acts were listed) are secondary to the prohibition itself.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 5 absolute prohibitions on specific AI practices

requirements.title: Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
requirements.summary: Classifies AI systems as high-risk by reference to Annex III use cases and to AI that is a safety component of products covered by Union harmonization legislation.

moral_profile.rationale: Risk class follows foreseeable harm potential of the use case or product role, not the character of the provider or a blanket ban on a technique.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 6 and Annex III harm-based high-risk classification

requirements.title: Risk management system
requirements.summary: Requires a continuous iterative risk management system for high-risk AI, including identification, estimation, mitigation, and residual-risk acceptance.

moral_profile.rationale: The organizing logic is residual risk to health, safety, and fundamental rights. Mandatory process steps are the means; named provider duties are the carrier of those means.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 9 continuous risk management keyed to foreseeable harms

requirements.title: Data and data governance
requirements.summary: Training, validation, and testing data for high-risk AI must meet quality criteria, including relevance, representativeness, and examination for bias.

moral_profile.rationale: Provider data-governance duties (actor) and mandated examination practices (action) both serve bias and performance outcomes. No single dimension dominates.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 10 data quality and bias-examination duties on providers

requirements.title: Technical documentation
requirements.summary: The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system must be drawn up before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and it must be kept up to date. It must show that the system complies with the requirements in Section 2, give national competent authorities and notified bodies the information needed to assess that compliance, and contain at least the elements in Annex IV. SMEs, including start-ups, and SMCs may provide those elements in a simplified manner, using the form the Commission establishes. Where the system is related to a product covered by the Union harmonization legislation in Section A of Annex I, one set of technical documentation contains the information in paragraph 1 and the information required under those acts.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaced the text of Article 11(1) after the first sentence, through the rule on the simplified form for SMEs, including start-ups, and SMCs. Paragraphs 2 and 3 are marked as the original text.

requirements.title: Record-keeping
requirements.summary: A high-risk AI system must technically allow the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system. Logging must make it possible to record events relevant to identifying situations that may result in the system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) or in a substantial modification, to facilitating the post-market monitoring in Article 72, and to monitoring the operation of systems under Article 26(5). For systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, the logs must include the period of each use, the reference database against which input data has been checked, the input data for which the search led to a match, and the identification of the natural persons involved in verifying the results under Article 14(5).
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text does not mark Article 12 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Transparency and provision of information to deployers
requirements.summary: A high-risk AI system must be designed and developed so that its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately. The system must be accompanied by instructions for use that include the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorized representative; the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, including accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity; known or foreseeable circumstances that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights; the human oversight measures; the computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and maintenance measures; and, where relevant, how deployers collect, store and interpret the logs.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text does not mark Article 13 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Human oversight
requirements.summary: High-risk AI must be designed so natural persons can oversee it effectively, including the ability to intervene or interrupt.

moral_profile.rationale: The core duty is to build and operate a human-oversight gate. Competence of the overseer matters, but the requirement is structured as a mandatory process and design rule.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 14 human oversight and intervene/interrupt capabilities

requirements.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
requirements.summary: High-risk AI must achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and be resilient against errors, faults, and unauthorized attempts to alter use or performance.

moral_profile.rationale: Performance and resilience thresholds against foreseeable failure and attack modes are the organizing logic. Process and provider duties exist to produce those outcomes.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 15 accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity performance duties

requirements.title: Obligations of providers of high-risk AI systems
requirements.summary: Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure that the system complies with the requirements in Section 2; indicate their name, trade name or trademark and a contact address on the system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or accompanying documentation; keep a quality management system that complies with Article 17; keep the documentation referred to in Article 18; keep the logs referred to in Article 19 when those logs are under their control; have the system undergo the conformity assessment in Article 43 before it is placed on the market or put into service; draw up an EU declaration of conformity under Article 47; affix the CE marking under Article 48; comply with the registration obligations in Article 49(1); take the corrective actions and provide the information required in Article 20; demonstrate conformity with Section 2 on a reasoned request from a national competent authority; and ensure that the system complies with the accessibility requirements in Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text does not mark Article 16 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Quality management system
requirements.summary: Providers of high-risk AI systems must put in place a quality management system, documented in written policies, procedures and instructions. It includes at least a strategy for regulatory compliance and for managing modifications; design control and design verification; development, quality control and quality assurance; examination, test and validation procedures; technical specifications; data-management procedures; the risk management system in Article 9; the post-market monitoring system in Article 72; procedures for reporting a serious incident under Article 73; communication with authorities, notified bodies, other operators, customers or other interested parties; record-keeping; resource management, including security-of-supply measures; and an accountability framework for management and other staff. Implementation is proportionate to the size of the provider's organization, including where the provider is an SME, a start-up or an SMC, and the provider must still meet the degree of rigor and the level of protection required for compliance. A provider already subject to a quality management system or an equivalent function under sectoral Union law may include these aspects in that system. For a financial institution, the duty is deemed fulfilled by compliance with the applicable Union financial-services rules on internal governance, except for paragraph 1, points (g), (h) and (i).
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaced Article 17(2).

requirements.title: Responsibilities along the AI value chain
requirements.summary: A distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is considered a provider of a high-risk AI system, and is subject to the Article 16 obligations, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system already placed on the market or put into service, makes a substantial modification to such a system so that it remains high-risk under Article 6, or modifies the intended purpose of a system that was not high-risk so that the system becomes high-risk under Article 6. Where that happens, the provider that initially placed the system on the market or put it into service is no longer considered the provider of that specific system. That initial provider must cooperate with the new providers and make available the necessary information, reasonably expected technical access and other assistance, including technical documentation sufficient to assess compliance with Article 16, information on known limitations and failure modes, and targeted technical access for testing and validation. That cooperation duty does not apply where the initial provider has clearly specified that its system is not to be changed into a high-risk AI system. For a high-risk system that is a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonization legislation in Section A of Annex I, the product manufacturer is considered the provider when the system is placed on the market or put into service under the manufacturer's name or trademark. The provider of a high-risk system and a third party that supplies an AI system, AI model, tools, services, components or processes that are used or integrated in that system must, by written agreement, specify the information, capabilities, technical access and other assistance needed for the provider to comply. Paragraph 4 does not apply to third parties that make tools, services, processes or components, other than general-purpose AI models, accessible to the public under a free and open-source license.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaced Article 25(2) and Article 25(4).

requirements.title: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
requirements.summary: Deployers must assign human oversight, ensure input data relevance, monitor operation, and keep logs, among other duties.

moral_profile.rationale: The article assigns a bundle of duties to the deployer role. Process and monitoring requirements are substantial, but the defining move is naming who is obligated.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 26 deployer obligations

requirements.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment for high-risk AI systems
requirements.summary: Before deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), except a system intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of systems referred to in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III, must assess the impact on fundamental rights that the use of the system may produce. The assessment describes the deployer's processes, the period and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm, the human oversight measures, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialize, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms. The obligation applies to the first use. The deployer may rely on a previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessment or an existing impact assessment carried out by the provider in similar cases, and must update the information when a listed element has changed or is no longer up to date. After the assessment, the deployer notifies the market surveillance authority of the results, using the template in paragraph 5, unless Article 46(1) exempts that notification. Where an obligation in this article is already met by a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680, the deployer may include cross-references or the relevant parts. The AI Office develops a template for a questionnaire, including through an automated tool.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaced Article 27(4) and Article 27(5).

requirements.title: Notifying authorities
requirements.summary: Each Member State must designate or establish at least one notifying authority responsible for the procedures to assess, designate, notify and monitor conformity assessment bodies. Member States may have a national accreditation body carry out the assessment and monitoring. The notifying authority must be organized so that no conflict of interest arises with conformity assessment bodies, so that notification decisions are taken by competent persons different from those who carried out the assessment, and so that the authority does not offer conformity-assessment activities or consultancy services on a commercial or competitive basis. It must safeguard the confidentiality of information it obtains and must have an adequate number of competent personnel. Where a body applies for designation under this Regulation and under the Union harmonization legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, and that legislation provides for it, the notifying authorities must provide a single application and a unified assessment procedure. A notifying authority designated under that legislation is also the notifying authority for that procedure, unless the Member State designates another authority for this Regulation.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 inserted Article 28(8) and Article 28(9).

requirements.title: Conformity assessment
requirements.summary: For a high-risk AI system listed in point 1 of Annex III, the provider chooses internal control under Annex VI or an assessment of the quality management system and the technical documentation by a notified body under Annex VII, according to whether the provider has applied the relevant harmonized standards or common specifications. For systems referred to in points 2 to 8 of Annex III, the provider follows the internal-control procedure in Annex VI, which does not involve a notified body. For a high-risk system covered by the Union harmonization legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the provider follows the conformity assessment required under that legislation, and the requirements in Section 2 of this Chapter are part of that assessment. A system that has already undergone a conformity assessment undergoes a new one if it is substantially modified. For a system that continues to learn after being placed on the market or put into service, changes that the provider pre-determined at the initial assessment and that are part of the information in point 2(f) of Annex IV do not constitute a substantial modification.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 replaced Article 43(3).

requirements.title: EU declaration of conformity
requirements.summary: The provider must draw up a written machine-readable, physical or electronically signed EU declaration of conformity for each high-risk AI system, and keep it at the disposal of the national competent authorities for 10 years after the system has been placed on the market or put into service. The declaration identifies the system. A copy is submitted to the relevant national competent authorities on request. The declaration states that the system meets the requirements in Section 2, contains the information set out in Annex V, and is translated into a language easily understood by the authorities of the Member States where the system is placed on the market or made available. Where other Union harmonization legislation also requires an EU declaration of conformity, a single declaration is drawn up for all Union law applicable to the system. By drawing up the declaration, the provider assumes responsibility for compliance with the requirements in Section 2, and the provider keeps the declaration up to date.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text does not mark Article 47 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Registration
requirements.summary: Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, other than a system referred to in point 2 of Annex III, the provider or, where applicable, the authorized representative registers themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Article 71. Before placing on the market or putting into service a system that the provider has concluded is not high-risk under Article 6(3), that provider or authorized representative registers themselves and that system in the same database. Before putting into service or using a high-risk system listed in Annex III, other than point 2, deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, or persons acting on their behalf, register themselves, select the system and register its use. For systems referred to in points 1, 6 and 7 of Annex III, in law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control management, registration under paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 is in a secure non-public section of the database and includes only the information this article lists. High-risk systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III are registered at national level.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text does not mark Article 49 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Classification of general-purpose AI models as general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
requirements.summary: A general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks, or if, on a decision of the Commission taken on its own or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those, having regard to the criteria in Annex XIII. A model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25. The Commission adopts delegated acts to amend the thresholds in paragraphs 1 and 2 and to supplement benchmarks and indicators in light of technological developments.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text prints the training-computation threshold as "10 25", the Official Journal superscript. This summary writes that figure as 10^25. The consolidated text does not mark Article 51 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Procedure
requirements.summary: Where a general-purpose AI model meets the condition in Article 51(1), point (a), the provider notifies the Commission without delay and in any event within two weeks after that requirement is met or it becomes known that it will be met. The notification includes the information necessary to demonstrate that the requirement has been met. The provider may present, with the notification, arguments that the model does not present systemic risks because of its specific characteristics and therefore should not be classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk. If the Commission concludes that those arguments are not sufficiently substantiated, it rejects them and the model is considered a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk. The Commission may designate a model as presenting systemic risks, on its own or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, on the basis of the criteria in Annex XIII. A provider whose model was designated under paragraph 4 may request a reassessment at the earliest six months after the designation decision. The Commission publishes a list of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk and keeps that list up to date.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text does not mark Article 52 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models
requirements.summary: GPAI model providers must draw up technical documentation, publish a training-data summary, and cooperate with downstream providers, with additional duties for systemic-risk models.

moral_profile.rationale: Duties attach to the GPAI provider role (documentation, transparency, cooperation). Systemic-risk overlays add outcome pressure, but the article is structured as provider obligations.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 53 GPAI provider obligations

requirements.title: Post-market monitoring by providers
requirements.summary: Providers of high-risk AI must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportional to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk system.

moral_profile.rationale: Continuous observation of real-world performance and emerging harms is the point. Provider and process duties exist to make that observation happen.
moral_profile.evidence: Art. 72 post-market monitoring system

requirements.title: Reporting of serious incidents
requirements.summary: Providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market must report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States where that incident occurred. The report is made immediately after the provider has established a causal link between the AI system and the serious incident, or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and in any event not later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer becomes aware of the incident. For a widespread infringement or a serious incident as defined in Article 3, point (49)(b), the report is provided immediately and not later than two days after awareness. Where a person has died, the report is provided immediately after the provider or the deployer has established, or as soon as it suspects, a causal relationship, and not later than 10 days after awareness. An initial incomplete report may be followed by a complete report. After reporting, the provider investigates the incident and the system, including a risk assessment and corrective action, and cooperates with the competent authorities and, where relevant, the notified body. The article also sets the notice duties of the market surveillance authority and of national competent authorities toward the Commission, and it limits notification of serious incidents for certain Annex III systems and for systems covered by Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and (EU) 2017/746 to those referred to in Article 3, point (49)(c).
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text does not mark Article 73 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Right to explanation of individual decision-making
requirements.summary: Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer on the basis of the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, other than systems listed under point 2, and which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects that person in a way that they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety or fundamental rights, has the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken. Paragraph 1 does not apply to the use of AI systems for which exceptions from, or restrictions to, that obligation follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law. This article applies only to the extent that the right in paragraph 1 is not otherwise provided for under Union law.
requirements.source_note: Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 dated 2026-07-27 (02024R1689), which includes amending Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. EUR-Lex was not fetched. The consolidated text does not mark Article 86 with an M1 amendment from Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

requirements.title: Robustness, security and safety
requirements.summary: AI systems should be robust, secure, and safe throughout their lifecycle so that in conditions of normal use, foreseeable use or misuse, or other adverse conditions, they function appropriately and do not pose unreasonable safety risk. Includes the capacity to override, repair, and decommission.

moral_profile.rationale: The principle is framed around foreseeable adverse conditions and unreasonable safety risk. Override, repair, and decommission are mandated capabilities in service of that outcome. Cross-cutting soft law that most national robustness rules reuse.
moral_profile.evidence: OECD AI Principle 1.4 robustness, security, safety, and override/repair/decommission

requirements.title: Accountability
requirements.summary: AI actors should be accountable for the proper functioning of AI systems and for respect of the OECD AI Principles, based on their roles and the context.

moral_profile.rationale: Accountability attaches to AI actors according to role and context. The principle names who must answer, not which acts are banned or which harm thresholds apply.
moral_profile.evidence: OECD AI Principle 1.5 accountability of AI actors

requirements.title: Legal and regulatory requirements incorporated into AI risk policies
requirements.summary: Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood, managed, and documented.

moral_profile.rationale: Organizational duty to know and manage applicable AI law. The act of incorporating requirements into policy is mandated; harm outcomes are upstream of this control.
moral_profile.evidence: NIST AI RMF GOVERN 1.1

requirements.title: Roles and responsibilities for AI risk management
requirements.summary: Roles and responsibilities for AI risk and the AI risk management function are defined, assigned, and documented.

moral_profile.rationale: The requirement is to name accountable roles. Process documentation is the vehicle; outcome thresholds are not the subject.
moral_profile.evidence: NIST AI RMF GOVERN 2.1

requirements.title: AI system impacts on individuals, groups, and society
requirements.summary: Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized and documented.

moral_profile.rationale: Impact characterization is consequentialist by design: the requirement exists to surface foreseeable harms and benefits.
moral_profile.evidence: NIST AI RMF MAP 1.5

requirements.title: AI system privacy risk measurement
requirements.summary: AI system privacy risk is examined, documented, and managed based on assessments of privacy-related impacts.

moral_profile.rationale: Measurement is keyed to privacy-related impacts. Mandated assessment practice supports that outcome focus.
moral_profile.evidence: NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.6

requirements.title: Risk treatment responses documented and monitored
requirements.summary: Risk treatment responses, including residual risk acceptance, are documented, monitored, and communicated.

moral_profile.rationale: Residual risk acceptance and ongoing monitoring center foreseeable impacts. Named ownership and process steps carry the outcome duty.
moral_profile.evidence: NIST AI RMF MANAGE 2.4

requirements.title: Effective challenge
requirements.summary: Critical analysis by objective, informed parties that can identify model weaknesses and produce appropriate changes. Independence and competence of the challenger are central.

moral_profile.rationale: Effective challenge is defined by who challenges (informed, objective parties with stature) and the critical-analysis practice they must perform. Harm outcomes motivate the duty but do not structure the section.
moral_profile.evidence: SR 26-2 Section III effective challenge

requirements.title: Model development, implementation, and use
requirements.summary: Expectations for sound development, including conceptual soundness, data suitability, and appropriate use relative to model purpose.

moral_profile.rationale: The section mandates development and use practices. Outcome concerns (model purpose fitness) matter, but the text is organized as required process for building and deploying models.
moral_profile.evidence: SR 26-2 Section IV model development

requirements.title: Model validation and ongoing monitoring
requirements.summary: Independent validation and ongoing monitoring of model performance, including outcomes analysis and process verification.

moral_profile.rationale: Performance monitoring and outcomes analysis are the organizing logic. Independence of validators is a material actor duty supporting that outcome focus.
moral_profile.evidence: SR 26-2 Section V validation and ongoing monitoring

requirements.title: Governance, policies, and controls
requirements.summary: Board and senior management accountability, policies, controls, and model inventory expectations for the MRM framework.

moral_profile.rationale: Board and senior-management accountability and role clarity define the section. Policies and controls are the mandated acts those actors must maintain.
moral_profile.evidence: SR 26-2 Section VI governance and controls

requirements.title: Vendor and other third-party models
requirements.summary: Institutions remain responsible for MRM of vendor and third-party models commensurate with the models' risk, including due diligence and ongoing monitoring.

moral_profile.rationale: Responsibility stays with the institution regardless of who built the model. Due diligence and monitoring practices serve that accountability, with risk-commensurate intensity pointing at outcomes.
moral_profile.evidence: SR 26-2 Section VII vendor and third-party products

requirements.title: Principles relating to processing of personal data
requirements.summary: Lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality, and accountability for personal-data processing, including AI systems that process personal data.

moral_profile.rationale: Accountability and controller duties name who must comply; the principles are mandatory processing acts. Harm to data subjects motivates the regime but the article is organized as required practice plus accountable actors.
moral_profile.evidence: GDPR Art. 5 principles and accountability

requirements.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
requirements.summary: Gives data subjects rights against decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects, with limited exceptions and required safeguards.

moral_profile.rationale: The duty is structured as a prohibited or constrained act (solely automated significant decisions) plus contestability safeguards. Actor rights and significant effects are material but the organizing rule is the decision practice itself.
moral_profile.evidence: GDPR Art. 22 automated decision-making

requirements.title: Data protection impact assessment
requirements.summary: Requires a DPIA where processing, especially using new technologies, is likely to result in high risk to rights and freedoms of natural persons.

moral_profile.rationale: High-risk to rights and freedoms is the trigger. Mandatory assessment process and controller ownership carry that outcome focus.
moral_profile.evidence: GDPR Art. 35 DPIA

requirements.title: Administrative safeguards
requirements.summary: Requires covered entities and business associates to implement administrative safeguards (risk analysis, workforce security, contingency planning, evaluation) for ePHI.

moral_profile.rationale: Named organizational duties and mandated safeguard practices dominate. Confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI are the protected outcomes those acts serve.
moral_profile.evidence: HIPAA Security Rule 45 CFR 164.308

requirements.title: Technical safeguards
requirements.summary: Requires access control, audit controls, integrity controls, and transmission security for electronic protected health information.

moral_profile.rationale: The section mandates specific technical control practices. Outcomes (protect ePHI) motivate the rule; named actors are secondary to the required safeguards.
moral_profile.evidence: HIPAA Security Rule 45 CFR 164.312

requirements.title: Cross-cutting principles for UK AI regulation
requirements.summary: Sets five principles delivered through existing sector regulators rather than a single AI Act: safety/security/robustness, transparency, fairness, accountability/governance, and contestability/redress.

moral_profile.rationale: Accountability and governance name who must act inside existing regulator remits. Safety and fairness point at outcomes; transparency and contestability are mandated process rights.
moral_profile.evidence: UK AI white paper five principles

requirements.title: Sector regulators deliver AI duties
requirements.summary: Rejects a single horizontal AI statute in favor of existing sector regulators applying the five principles in context.

moral_profile.rationale: The design choice is who enforces (existing sector regulators and accountable firms). Process adaptation inside remits is secondary; harm outcomes are left to sector context.
moral_profile.evidence: UK AI white paper regulator-led approach

requirements.title: Lawful training data and security assessment
requirements.summary: Requires generative AI providers to use training data from lawful sources, respect IP and personal information rules, and complete security assessments for public-facing services.

moral_profile.rationale: Mandatory provider practices for data and assessment dominate. Provider identity matters; content and rights harms motivate the duties.
moral_profile.evidence: China GenAI Interim Measures training-data and assessment duties

requirements.title: Synthetic content labeling and safety
requirements.summary: Requires labeling of generated content and measures to prevent generation of illegal or harmful content by public generative AI services.

moral_profile.rationale: Labeling and content-safety bans are mandated acts aimed at preventing harmful outputs. Provider role is the carrier, not the moral center.
moral_profile.evidence: China GenAI Interim Measures labeling and content safety

requirements.title: Algorithmic Impact Assessment requirement
requirements.summary: Requires federal institutions to complete an Algorithmic Impact Assessment before production use of an automated decision system, with impact level driving peer review and transparency duties.

moral_profile.rationale: Impact level and foreseeable effects on clients organize the duty. Named institutional owners and mandatory AIA process support that outcome focus.
moral_profile.evidence: Canada Directive on ADM Algorithmic Impact Assessment

requirements.title: Transparency and explanation to affected persons
requirements.summary: Requires plain-language notice that a decision will be automated and meaningful explanations of how and why the decision was made, scaled to impact level.

moral_profile.rationale: Notice and explanation are mandated communicative acts. Institutional accountability and client impact are material supports.
moral_profile.evidence: Canada Directive on ADM transparency duties

requirements.title: Access control for CUI environments
requirements.summary: Requires limiters on system access to authorized users and processes protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in defense contractor environments.

moral_profile.rationale: Required access-control practices are the organizing logic. Named contractor accountability and CUI confidentiality outcomes support those acts.
moral_profile.evidence: CMMC 2.0 Access Control practices

requirements.title: Audit logging and accountability
requirements.summary: Requires create, protect, and retain system audit records so actions affecting CUI systems can be traced to accountable parties.

moral_profile.rationale: Traceability to accountable parties is the moral center. Mandatory logging practices implement that actor duty; mission harm is upstream context.
moral_profile.evidence: CMMC 2.0 Audit and Accountability

requirements.title: Firm vs investor conflicts in PDA/AI tools
requirements.summary: Proposed SEC approach would require firms to eliminate or neutralize conflicts when predictive analytics or similar AI optimizations place firm interests ahead of investor interests.

moral_profile.rationale: The proposed duty targets harmful conflict outcomes for investors and mandates elimination or neutralization practices. Firm accountability is the carrier.
moral_profile.evidence: SEC PDA conflicts proposed rule investor-interest framing

requirements.title: National AI governance structure
requirements.summary: Establishes national AI governance bodies and policy coordination duties for the Korean government and covered AI businesses.

moral_profile.rationale: Named national and organizational accountability is the primary orientation. Process and risk duties follow from that structure.
moral_profile.evidence: Korea AI Basic Act governance provisions

requirements.title: Transparency and safety obligations
requirements.summary: Imposes transparency and safety-related duties on AI businesses, with higher expectations where systems can significantly affect rights or safety.

moral_profile.rationale: Mandated transparency and safety practices aim at preventing significant rights and safety harms. Business accountability is material but secondary to the required acts and outcomes.
moral_profile.evidence: Korea AI Basic Act transparency and safety duties

requirements.title: Accountability principle
requirements.summary: Those responsible for AI systems should be identifiable and accountable for the outcomes of the AI systems, with appropriate human oversight.

moral_profile.rationale: Identifiable responsible parties define the principle. Oversight practices and outcome ownership are supporting duties.
moral_profile.evidence: Australia AI Ethics Principles accountability

requirements.title: Contestability principle
requirements.summary: When an AI system significantly affects a person, there should be timely processes to allow people to challenge use or outcomes of the AI system.

moral_profile.rationale: The principle mandates contestation processes for significant AI effects. Affected persons and harm stakes matter; the organizing requirement is the challenge practice.
moral_profile.evidence: Australia AI Ethics Principles contestability

requirements.title: Conduct pre-deployment testing
requirements.summary: Section 4(b) of M-25-21 lists this as the first minimum practice for high-impact AI. Agencies must develop pre-deployment testing and prepare risk mitigation plans that reflect expected real-world outcomes and identify expected benefits of the AI use.
requirements.source_note: Quoted from M-25-21 heading 4.b, fetched 2026-11-15. The memorandum lists the practices in order under Section 4(b). Control files cite that order as Section 4(b)(i), (ii), and (iii).

requirements.title: Complete an AI impact assessment
requirements.summary: Section 4(b) of M-25-21 lists this as the second minimum practice. Agencies must complete an AI impact assessment before deploying any high-impact AI use case. The assessment is documented and updated through the lifecycle.
requirements.source_note: Quoted from M-25-21 heading 4.b, fetched 2026-11-15. The memorandum lists the practices in order under Section 4(b). Control files cite that order as Section 4(b)(i), (ii), and (iii).

requirements.title: Conduct ongoing monitoring
requirements.summary: Section 4(b) of M-25-21 lists this as the third minimum practice. Agencies must conduct testing and periodic human review, where feasible, to identify adverse impacts on the performance and security of AI, including impacts that may violate laws governing privacy, civil rights, or civil liberties.
requirements.source_note: Quoted from M-25-21 heading 4.b, fetched 2026-11-15. The memorandum lists the practices in order under Section 4(b). Control files cite that order as Section 4(b)(i), (ii), and (iii).

citation_match_note: citation_match patterns are tested only against citations filed under the mapping_key of this requirement's own instrument. Cross-instrument text collisions therefore cannot create an implements edge, so patterns can stay readable. Patterns must match the citation text a control actually writes: an instrument name alone will not match a schema that cites clause IDs. Requirements listed in unmatched_expected are known to have no implementing control; the verifier fails on any other requirement whose instrument is cited but whose patterns match nothing, and on stale entries that have since matched.
